course: Packaging and Publishing an Online Course on Udemy
lesson_title: Write learning objectives with Bloom's taxonomy
learners: Teachers, lecturers, trainers and coaches building their first online course; used to writing aims in lesson plans, never wrote measurable objectives
test_title: End-of-lesson test: Bloom's taxonomy and the objective formula
timing: After Video 6, before the assignment is submitted
conditions: Closed book; the short-answer part is done after the selected-response part is handed in
instructions: The test has five parts. Parts A to D are selected-response, 0.4 points per item, 15 minutes. Part E is one short-answer question worth 1.6 points, 10 minutes. Write your answers on the answer sheet, not on the test.

pass_mark.reason: Objectives K1 and K2 both set a standard of 8/10, and 80% is the usual pass mark for Udemy quizzes.

objectives.text: Describe the 6 cognitive levels of the 2001 Bloom's taxonomy in the correct order, with at least 3 action verbs for each level, closed book, scoring at least 8/10
Tell correctly written objectives from faulty ones in a given list of 10, naming the fault in each faulty objective, at least 8/10
Write at least 3 course-level objectives and 1 objective per lesson for their own course on the objective table provided, each with all 4 components and at the planned Bloom level
Score their own objective table with the 6-criterion checklist, record the faults and rewrite every objective that fails before submitting
Remove every unmeasurable verb from the submitted table and revise on the instructor's feedback within 1 week

topics.name: The 5-step process for an objective table (Video 5)

items.stem: The version of Bloom's taxonomy used in curriculum documents today is a revision by whom, and in which year?
items.explanation: 1956 is Bloom's original. The version in use is the 2001 revision edited by Anderson and Krathwohl. Mager wrote about behavioural objectives and Dale drew the cone of experience; neither revised the taxonomy.

items.stem: What is the correct order of the six levels of the 2001 taxonomy, from lowest to highest?
options: Remember, Understand, Analyze, Apply, Evaluate, Create
Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyze, Evaluate, Create
Understand, Remember, Apply, Analyze, Create, Evaluate
Remember, Apply, Understand, Analyze, Evaluate, Create
items.explanation: Apply comes before Analyze: you can do a familiar task before you can take its structure apart. The other options swap Remember and Understand or Evaluate and Create, the two places learners mix up most.

items.stem: What is the biggest change in the 2001 taxonomy compared with the 1956 original?
options: Remember was dropped as unnecessary for adults
A seventh level was added for emotions
Levels became verbs, and Create moved to the top
Understand and Apply were merged into one level
items.explanation: The 2001 revision renamed the levels from nouns (Knowledge) to verbs (Remember) to stress what the learner does, and put Synthesis, renamed Create, at the top. No level was dropped or merged.

items.stem: At which Bloom level is the objective "Point out where the questions become chained in a given 8-minute video of a lesson"?
items.explanation: The learner has to break the lesson into its questions and find the faulty spot, which is Analyze. Understand would only ask what chained questions are; Apply would be writing questions from a model; Create would be designing a new question set.

items.stem: Which verb below should NOT open a learning objective?
items.explanation: "Grasp" belongs with understand, know and be aware of: it does not say what the learner will do so you can check it. The other three verbs are on the Bloom verb sheet.

items.stem: At which level is the objective "Compare two ways of opening a lesson against 3 criteria and choose the one that suits your class"?
items.explanation: There are criteria and there is a choice, so the learner judges value: Evaluate. Comparing without choosing would be Analyze. Many people pick Analyze because they see the word "compare".

items.stem: Why is the verb "understand" kept out of the start of an objective?
options: It does not say how the objective will be checked
items.explanation: An action verb is the check written into the objective. "Understand" is a fine word, but the moment you test it you have to swap it for name, explain or sort. No regulation forbids it; regulations ask for measurable verbs.

items.stem: In step 2 of the objective-table process, at which level should the first lessons of a course usually sit?
options: Levels 1 to 2, rising towards the end
Level 3, to match every other lesson
items.explanation: A course climbs: low at the start, high at the end, and the last lesson has a product at level 5 or 6. A course where every lesson sits at the same level is flat; push one or two final lessons up.

items.stem: All four objectives below use the verb "write". Which one is at the Create level?
options: Write one objective from a given sentence pattern
Write the full objective set for a new course of your own
Write a model sentence again in your own words
Write titles for 5 videos that already exist
items.explanation: The level comes from what the learner does with knowledge, not from the verb. Writing a whole set for a new course builds a new structure from many parts: Create. From a pattern is Apply; in your own words is Understand; titling existing videos is routine Apply.

items.stem: How is "Describe" at the start of a knowledge objective in a vocational curriculum treated?
options: As a fault, it has to be replaced
As acceptable, at the Understand level
As one of the banned verbs
items.explanation: Describe is an action verb at the Understand level, common in vocational programs and checkable orally or in writing. It is nothing like understand, know or grasp.

items.stem: Hannah, a Year 9 teacher in Leeds, writes this objective for her online course: "Learners will grasp how to ask open questions." Which fault should she fix first?
options: It is written from the teacher's side
items.explanation: "Grasp" makes the whole objective uncheckable, so it goes first. The object is there (how to ask open questions) and it is written from the learner's side. The missing condition is the second fix.

items.stem: You score "Help learners know how to write objectives" with the 6-criterion checklist. Which result is correct?
options: Fails criterion 6 only: two tasks in one line
Fails criteria 1 and 6: "know" and the teacher's side
items.explanation: "Help" is the teacher's job, not the learner's (criterion 6), and "know" cannot be measured (criterion 1). There is only one task, so it does not fail for two tasks. It also lacks a standard, but the option claiming criterion 4 alone misses both real faults.
items.source: Video 6, section 3.4, scoring demo table A

items.stem: A learner submits the objective "Design effective slides". Which criterion does it fail most clearly?
options: Two different tasks are joined with "and"
It is written from the instructor's side
items.explanation: Design is a good action verb. The fault is "effective": you cannot count it or see it, so swap it for a number of slides, lines, colours or a template. The object and condition are thin too, but criterion 4 is the obvious failure.
items.source: Video 4, section 2.3, slide 14 on the 6 kinds of standard

items.stem: Marco teaches office software in Bologna and writes: "Write a video script and record an 8-minute video." What is wrong with it?
options: Two tasks that are checked apart share one line
There is no standard for length
items.explanation: The script is handed in first and the video later, each checked with a different tool, so they need two lines (criterion 6). The verbs and the 8-minute standard are fine.
items.source: Video 6, section 3.4, scoring demo table B

items.stem: How does the objective "List the 6 levels of the 2001 Bloom's taxonomy in the correct order, closed book" score on the 6-criterion checklist?
options: Fails criterion 5: verb at the wrong level
items.explanation: Verb list (Remember), object the 6 levels, condition closed book, standard correct order, one task, learner's side. All 6. People who pick a fault usually miss that "closed book" is the condition and "correct order" is the standard.

items.stem: Priya, a soft-skills trainer in Pune, writes "Design 10 beautiful slides for the lecture". When she scores it herself, which criterion should she mark as failed?
options: Criterion 6, written from the teacher's side
items.explanation: The object is there (10 slides), the verb is there (design), the side is right. "Beautiful" is a judgement, so replace it: one idea per slide, at most 6 lines, at most 3 colours, on the slide master made earlier.

items.stem: The objective "Turn 10 given closed questions into open questions, 10/10 of them impossible to answer with yes or no" already has a countable standard.
items.explanation: 10/10 together with the sign "impossible to answer with yes or no" is a standard of the number-plus-observable-quality kind.

items.stem: The line "Bloom's taxonomy 2001" passes as an objective because it names the lesson content correctly.
items.explanation: That is a content heading, not an objective: no verb, nothing the learner does. It is fault number 1 in the table of common mistakes.

items.stem: An objective table for a Udemy course should end up with 3 to 5 course-level objectives, each tied to a real product the learner submits.
items.explanation: Step 4 of the process: gather 3 to 5 course-level objectives from the largest products; write the check first, then the objective. A table with 8 to 11 lines is the greedy-table mistake.

items.stem: Match each objective on the left with the correct scoring result on the right.
left: Be aware of the importance of objectives
Write 3 course-level objectives on the template, each with all 4 components
right: Fails 1 and 4: unmeasurable verb, no standard
Fails 3 and 4: no scoring tool, no result to count
Fails 6: two tasks in one line
Fails 5: verb at the wrong Bloom level
items.explanation: Line 1 uses "be aware of" and has no standard. Line 2 has verb, object, condition (the template) and standard (all 4 components). Line 3 has a good verb but says neither what it is scored with nor what the result looks like; rewrite as "using the 6-criterion checklist, naming the failed criterion of each line".

items.stem: A complete learning objective has four components: an action verb, an object, a ____ and a ____.
items.explanation: The formula is verb + object + condition, tool or context + standard. The two blanks may come in either order.

items.stem: Tom teaches air-conditioning repair at a college in Cardiff and is building his first Udemy course. His lesson objective reads: "Help learners understand the refrigerant charging procedure." Rewrite it as one objective with all 4 components, at the Apply level.
items.requirements: 1 or 2 sentences, at most 60 words, 10 minutes. Scored on the 4 points below, not on air-conditioning knowledge.

scoring.point: A measurable action verb at the Apply level (carry out, charge, complete); no "help" or "understand" left
A concrete object: the charging procedure for a named unit, a number of steps or the procedure's name
A condition or tool: on which training rig, with a manifold gauge set, following the procedure sheet
A countable standard: correct order of N steps, pressure inside a given range, a time limit, no safety breach

items.model_answer: Carry out the 7-step R32 charging procedure on a 9,000 BTU wall-mounted training unit, using a manifold gauge set and the procedure sheet, in the correct order, with suction pressure between 110 and 130 psi, within 30 minutes and with no safety breach.
items.explanation: 0.4 per point; give 0.2 when the point is there but vague (for example "correct technique" with no number).

assignments.title: Write and self-score the objective table for your course
assignments.task: Follow the 5 steps for your own course. (1) For each lesson in your course map, write one plain sentence about what the learner can do afterwards. (2) Give each a Bloom level, with at least 3 different levels across the course. (3) Rewrite each sentence with the 4-component formula and stop to check before step 4. (4) Gather 3 to 5 course-level objectives, each tied to a product the learner hands in. (5) Score the whole table with the 6-criterion checklist and fill in the Rewrite as column for every line below 6/6, including the objective you wrote in Video 1. Submit both files to the lesson's assignment.
assignments.conditions: Use the course map from M01 Lesson 2, the objective table template (task sheet M02-L1-2) and the checklist (check sheet M02-L1-3). If you have no course map yet, use the sample course Asking questions in class (handout M02-L1-4).
assignments.deliverable: File 1: the objective table (.docx or .xlsx from the template) with 3 to 5 course-level objectives and 1 to 2 objectives per lesson, with a Bloom level column. File 2: the completed 6-criterion checklist for every line, with a Rewrite as column.
assignments.deadline: 7 days after the lesson opens; the revision after instructor feedback within the next 7 days
assignments.marker: Self-scored with this rubric before submitting, then scored by the instructor within 7 days, who names at most 3 major faults and rewrites one line as a model

criteria.name: Measurable verbs at the right Bloom level (S1, A1)
descriptors: More than 2 lines still use a banned verb (understand, know, grasp, be aware of, become familiar with), or fewer than 50% of lines sit at the planned level
No banned verbs; 50 to 80% of lines at the level given in the Bloom column
No banned verbs; over 80% of lines at the right level, at least 3 different levels in the course
Every line has a measurable verb at the right level; the final lesson has a level 5 or 6 objective tied to a real product

criteria.name: All 4 components, countable standards (S1)
descriptors: Fewer than 50% of lines have all 4 components
50 to 80% of lines have all 4 components; more than 2 standards still say good, effective or appropriate
Over 80% of lines have all 4 components; no more than 2 standards are still vague
Every line has all 4 components; every standard is a number, time, template, ratio or sequence

criteria.name: Course coverage and course-level objectives (S1)
descriptors: More than 2 lessons have no objective, or there are no course-level objectives
1 or 2 lessons missing; course-level objectives exist but fall outside 3 to 5 lines
Every lesson covered; 3 to 5 course-level objectives, but 1 line has no product to hand in
Every lesson covered; 3 to 5 course-level objectives, each tied to a product that can be handed in

criteria.name: Honest self-scoring, rewriting and deadlines (S2, A1)
descriptors: No checklist submitted, or submitted more than 3 days late
Checklist submitted but 3 or more lines differ from the instructor's scoring, or some failed lines have no rewrite
No more than 2 lines differ from the instructor's scoring; every failed line rewritten, 1 or 2 rewrites still fail
No more than 1 line differs; every rewritten line passes 6/6; on time, and the revision after feedback arrives within 7 days

assignments.pass_rule: At least 6.5/10 with no criterion at Needs work, and no banned verb in the final file
assignments.self_check: Before submitting, mark your level on each criterion of this rubric and write it in the last box of the checklist. The instructor scores it again; the gap between your score and the instructor's is one line of criterion 4.
